name: Labret piercing

lead: A labret is a piercing below the lower lip, above the chin, usually fitted with a flat-backed stud. The word can also mean any ornament attached to the lip, and the style has long cultural history.
People wear one as a facial accent, with variants such as vertical labrets, snakebites, spiderbites and lowbrets. Some stretch the piercing to wear larger plugs.

paras: Initial piercings are usually 1.2, 1.6 or 2.0 mm in diameter and are performed by a piercer. Healing typically takes 6 to 9 months, after which the piercing can be gradually stretched.

A 2006 dental study of 91 pierced subjects found gum recession on teeth opposing the labret in 68 percent, versus 22 percent of unpierced controls. A 2024 case report described a large soft-tissue defect below the lip after sequential expansion.

angle.text: The jewelry is the aesthetic, a visible accent at the lower lip and chin. Dental research links labrets to gum recession on opposing teeth.

lead: A labret is a piercing below the bottom lip, above the chin. The word can also mean any ornament attached to the lip, and the piercing is also called a tongue pillar or soul patch piercing.[1]

People wear labrets as a facial accent and style marker. Contemporary variants include the vertical labret, snakebites, spiderbites and the lowbret placed low toward the chin, and the piercing can be stretched to hold plugs.[1] Labrets have deep history: on the Northwest Coast of North America they signaled status for thousands of years, Tlingit women wore them in Southeast Alaska, and the Aztecs called them tentetl, or lip stone.[1]
infobox: Below the lower lip, above the chin[1]

paras: On the Northwest Coast, labrets marked status for roughly 1,500 to 3,500 years before the present, and descendant communities still regard them as meaningful symbols of social identity.[1] Aztec labrets were linked to status, power and eloquence, and labrets appear in Moche art.[1] Wear patterns on teeth in a Late Pleistocene or Early Holocene Tanzanian skull resemble those caused by labrets, and a 14th-century Sao skull from Cameroon shows labret-related wear.[2][3]

Modern labrets include vertical labrets, snakebites, spiderbites, lowbrets and larger labret plugs, often over 10 mm.[1] Healing is reported to take 6 to 9 months, after which stretching is possible.[1]

A 2006 dental study compared 91 people with lip piercings and labrets against 54 unpierced controls. Gingival recession on teeth opposing the labret occurred in 68.13 percent of pierced subjects versus 22.2 percent of controls, with an odds ratio of 7.5; age, gender, smoking and labret configuration did not significantly affect recession.[4] A 2024 case report described a radiographic artifact from a large opening beneath the lower lip created by sequentially larger soft-tissue expanders.[5]
